1.title: Read the market for smart homes
1.intro: Smart condos add sensors, controls and data to ordinary flats.
pts: Buyers care about energy bills, security, comfort and resale value.
List features by cost and value: smart thermostat, leak sensors, access control, EV charging, shared-space booking.
Interview ten buyers or tenants: which features they would pay for.
Check local condo prices and absorption (units sold per month).
Walk two finished smart buildings and list what residents actually use and what sits idle.
Ask about winter: heating, ventilation and parking with a plug-in outlet matter more in cold regions. Write which feature solves a real winter problem.
Separate must-have features that every unit gets from optional upgrades that a buyer can add for a price.
1.ex: Leak sensors cost 80 per unit and cut insurance claims; buyers rank them above voice assistants. For a 40-unit building, 40 x 80 = 3,200 buys sensors for every unit, a small share of a 17.2M build cost.
1.act: Interview ten people and rank features by willingness to pay.

2.title: Know development rules
2.intro: Developers follow zoning, building and condo law.
pts: Zoning and official plans decide what you may build.
Building code and permits come before work; inspections follow.
Condo law (provincial) governs sale, deposits, disclosure and cooling-off.
Smart systems that collect resident data fall under privacy law.
Check what happens to each feature if the internet fails for a day.
Energy and accessibility rules in the building code affect your design; check the provincial code edition in force.
Check the provincial rule on how long deposits stay in trust and what must be disclosed to buyers before they sign.
2.ex: Row: 'Take buyer deposits | provincial condo law | hold in trust and give disclosure | before any sale | lawyer's trust account record'. If each of 40 units takes a deposit, there are 40 separate deposit records to reconcile with the trust account.
2.act: Build a rules table for a 40-unit building.
2.std: Rules cited with source and date.

3.title: Plan the building and the smart layer
3.intro: Design the shared network and standards first.
pts: Choose open standards so devices from different makers work together.
Plan cabling, power and network closets at design time.
Decide who owns data from sensors and who can see it.
Plan updates and support for ten years.
Ask the building operator who will pay for software updates in year 5.
Draw a floor plan marking every device, cable run, power point and network closet, and give each device a number.
Make every smart function work by hand if the network fails: lights, door locks and heating must still operate.
3.ex: Open standard chosen so that a failed hub vendor can be replaced without rewiring. If each of 8 units on a floor has 12 devices, the floor plan lists 8 x 12 = 96 devices, each with a power point, a network path and an owner.
3.act: Draw a one-page system plan for a floor.
3.std: Every device has a power, network and owner.

4.title: Cost the development
4.intro: Land, construction, soft costs and financing.
pts: Hard costs: construction. Soft costs: design, permits, fees, marketing.
Financing cost grows each month of delay.
Contingency of 10 to 15%.
Compute profit = sales - all costs.
Cost features per unit and per year, not only at purchase.
Run a stress case: costs up 10% and sales down 5%. Write the new profit and margin.
Check the provincial and municipal charges and taxes that apply to new buildings and add each to the soft costs.
4.ex: 40 units x 520,000 = 20.8M; cost per unit 430,000 = 17.2M; profit 3.6M (17%). With costs up 10%, cost is 18.92M and profit falls to 1.88M (9%). A 10 to 15% contingency on 17.2M is 1.72M to 2.58M, so it should be inside the budget. Teaching figures in CAD.
4.act: Build a development pro forma with a 10% cost rise case.

5.title: Manage construction and quality
5.intro: Quality is checked at each stage.
pts: Stage gates: foundation, frame, services, finishes.
Walk the site weekly with a checklist.
Test smart systems before handover.
Keep a defects list and close it with dates.
Photograph every wall before it is closed, so later repairs know where cables run.
Write the pass criteria for each gate before work starts, such as inspection signed and cable test records filed.
Do not let finishes start until services pass their test; fixing a hidden cable later costs more.
5.ex: Defect list: 62 items at handover walk; 55 closed in 14 days (89%); 7 still open and carried to a new dated list. Repeat the walk when the 7 are done and sign off only when the count is zero.

6.title: Sell, hand over and support
pts: Give plain disclosure and a demonstration unit.
Train residents to use systems.
Set a help desk and response times.
Collect satisfaction after 90 days.
Test each smart system with the owner's phone, not only the installer's.
Give each buyer a written handover pack: warranty terms, system guide, who to call and what the building owner can see.
Make sure features remain usable if a resident does not own a smartphone.
6.ex: Demo-unit visits: 120; offers 30; sales 22. Rates: offers 30/120 = 25%, sales 22/30 = 73%. 22 of 40 units sold is 55%, so 18 units remain to sell. If the sales team tracks this each week, it can see early whether the pace is on plan.

7.title: Manage data, safety and sustainability
pts: Collect only needed data; tell residents; allow deletion.
Secure networks and update devices.
Plan fire, flood and power-cut responses.
Aim for energy performance targets.
Give residents a one-page guide in English and French.
Change every default password before handover and keep an access list of who can open the system.
Review sensor and camera data rules once a year and tell residents what changed.
7.ex: Policy line: 'Camera data kept 30 days, viewed only after an incident.' A camera that records 30 days and is viewed twice a year, each time after an incident, leaves a short log of 2 entries that residents can ask to see.
7.act: Write a resident data note and risk register.

8.title: Pilot a floor and plan scale
pts: Pilot with 8 units for 90 days.
Measure energy savings, faults and satisfaction.
Stop rule: more than 3 faults per unit per month means redesign.
Plan the next phase.
Collect resident feedback at 30 and 90 days and file it.
Compare each pilot unit's energy use with a similar unit without the smart layer, using meter readings.
Log each fault with date, device, cause and fix time to see which device fails most.
8.ex: Energy savings 14%; faults 1.5 per unit per month, so 8 units give 12 faults a month, well under the stop line of 3 per unit (24 a month); proceed. If a unit used 900 kWh a month before, 14% is a saving of 126 kWh.

quiz: Why plan cabling at design time?
Devices from different makers work together and can be replaced.
The law requires it to protect buyers.
A check before the next stage starts.
What should residents be told about data?
What is collected, why and how to delete it.
What triggers a redesign in the pilot?
More than 3 faults per unit per month.
What is profit in a pro forma?
